claim-1.claim: We can now write a lot more code, but our engineering know-how hasn't grown nearly as fast.
body: As implementation gets cheaper, deciding what to build, understanding the system, and determining whether the result is acceptable become relatively more important.

claim-2.claim: Large systems are too complex for any one person or agent to understand in full.
body: Software engineering deals with scale through abstraction: preserving the information needed for a particular task while leaving unnecessary detail out. Without useful abstractions, humans and agents must repeatedly reconstruct important knowledge from code and other lower-level artifacts.
claim-2.figure_region: Scale × finite reasoning → New engineering imbalance

claim-3.claim: Models make important knowledge easier to reason about and reuse.
body: A model is a concise representation of some aspect of a system, chosen for an engineering purpose. It may be incomplete or approximate, but it must be useful for that purpose. Models let humans and agents reason about important properties without repeatedly reconstructing them from lower-level artifacts.

claim-4.claim: Important requirements should actually affect the work.
body: It is not enough to tell an agent what matters. We must also have probabilistic and deterministic means of checking the agent's output against those requirements.

claim-5.claim: Recurring failures should improve the engineering system.
body: When failures recur or engineers repeatedly supply the same judgment, fixing the immediate result is not enough. Governance conversion changes the engineering environment so that future work can inherit what was learned rather than rediscover it.
When those changes continue to save work or prevent failures, they become engineering capital. When the same reconstruction and judgment must instead be repeated, MAGE calls that engineering churn.
claim-5.figure_region: Governance conversion; Engineering Capital vs. Engineering Churn

claim-6.claim: When writing code gets easier, more of the hard work moves to figuring out what to build, whether it is right, and how to keep it that way.
body: Agents may increasingly help with that work too. The enduring engineering responsibility is deciding what matters, what evidence is sufficient, what can be delegated, and what tradeoffs are acceptable.

_summary_line: Model what matters. Check the work against what matters. Learn from failures. Build what you learn back into the engineering environment.

core_question.question: How do we safely grant autonomy to commodity intelligence?

through_line.text: How do we safely grant autonomy to commodity intelligence?
Make intent explicit in models the fleet reasons through, and make the environment enforce the obligations that matter.
When autonomy exposes a new failure class, convert the lesson into durable structure so the next agent inherits a safer, more capable world.
